entries.clue: Start playing with posh bloke, holding same points (3,3)

indicatorNotes.holding: Something holding a thing has it gripped inside, so the letters named next are written in between the letters of the word that holds them.

blocks.note: a toff is British slang for a moneyed, upper-class man
a point on the compass is E for east, and asking for the same one twice writes that letter down twice

annotation.surface: An upper-class chap who is level on the scoreboard joins in as the game gets under way.
annotation.walkthrough: Points in a grid are nearly always compass points, and saying they are the same is a quiet way of asking for one letter doubled. The enumeration splits a six-letter run into two words of three.
annotation.definitionFit: To tee off is to strike the first shot of a round of golf, so starting play is what the phrase says.

entries.clue: Beverages for the journalist being mocked (6)

blocks.note: cups of tea, counted
ED is the editor, the crossword's stock newspaperman

annotation.surface: Drinks are bought for the reporter everyone is laughing at.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue marks the join: the two pieces are simply written down in the order they are given. Journalist is one of a small set of words — editor, sub, hack — that a grid keeps handy for two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To tease someone is to mock them, gently or otherwise, and both words describe what is done to the butt of a joke.

entries.clue: Feature one in each herbal remedy (9)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the pieces already assembled inside the word that follows, which opens up to take them.

blocks.note: ea. is the price-label abbreviation for each
the chin is a feature of the face
the one on a playing card is the ace

annotation.surface: An instruction to include one of them in every bottle of the plant-based cure.
annotation.walkthrough: Feature points at a face rather than anything on a chemist's shelf, and one is the card rather than the digit. Echinacea is the purple coneflower, taken in drops and tablets against colds.
annotation.definitionFit: Echinacea is sold in health shops as a cold and flu preparation made from the coneflower, which is the herbal remedy meant.

entries.clue: Note, I have this number (4)

blocks.note: F is a note of the musical scale
I have contracts to I've, and a grid has no room for the apostrophe

annotation.surface: A memo pointing out the number already in hand.
annotation.walkthrough: Contractions are fair game in a grid, which is how two words become three letters. The comma after Note is punctuation, and a setter may put one wherever the surface reads best.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is the bare category — five is one of the counting numbers — with this pointing at the one just spelt out.

entries.clue: The last word on accepting copper shows shrewdness (6)

indicatorNotes.accepting: Something accepting takes another thing in, so the word before it opens up and the next piece sits inside.

blocks.note: amen is the word that closes a prayer
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

annotation.surface: Having the final say on a matter means taking a policeman's view on board.
annotation.walkthrough: Copper is the trap: the clue wants the metal in the periodic table, not the officer on the beat. On is doing surface work only, holding the phrase together without moving a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Acumen is sharp practical judgement — business acumen, political acumen — which is what shrewdness names.

entries.clue: Current units in quote for holiday area (8)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the piece before it inside the word after it, which splits open to take it.

blocks.note: to cite an authority is to quote it
amps are the units electric current is measured in

annotation.surface: Electricity usage written into the price quoted for somewhere to spend the summer.
annotation.walkthrough: Current is electrical here rather than up to date, and quote is the verb rather than the estimate a builder posts through the door. Both words keep the surface in an office and both belong to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A campsite is the field set aside for tents and caravans, so holiday area names it by what people use it for.

entries.clue: Encountered in some trouble (3)

indicatorNotes.in: In says the thing wanted is already sitting inside the words that follow, spelt out there without a letter changed.

blocks.note: the run straddles the gap between the two words: soME Trouble

annotation.surface: Running into somebody just as things were going wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: A three-letter answer with a word boundary to hide across is the classic shape for a concealment, because no single short word would hold it convincingly. The definition is the plain past tense of meet.
annotation.definitionFit: To have met someone is to have encountered them, the same act in the same tense.

entries.clue: Annoyed by informant and newspaperman (6)

blocks.note: a nark is British slang for a police informer, the grass who tells on his own
ED is the editor again, two letters every grid keeps in stock

annotation.surface: A grass and a press man between them have put somebody's back up.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves come from the same root: narked is what the nark leaves you feeling. By and and are joins that carry no letters, which is why the clue reads as a sentence rather than a sum.
annotation.definitionFit: Narked is British slang for irritated — he was well narked about it — which is annoyed with the temperature turned down a little.

entries.clue: Tree has fallen (3)

indicatorNotes.fallen: Something fallen has come down in a heap, and letters in a heap are no longer standing in the order they were given.

blocks.note: three letters of fodder, the whole of the answer's length

annotation.surface: News that a tree has come down.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words, and the fodder is the smallest and least noticeable of them, which is why the clue reads as a bulletin rather than an instruction. Fallen is doing the shuffling; it is not describing the tree.
annotation.definitionFit: The ash is a tall hedgerow and woodland tree, so the bare word tree names it by its kind.

entries.clue: Cellar length, say, of potential gauge? (9)

indicatorNotes.say: Say marks the words beside it as things to be heard rather than read, so you take the noise and write it down another way.

blocks.note: a cellar is a vault, and the spelling the grid wants for that sound is the electrical unit
the metre is the unit of length, respelt the American way

annotation.surface: The measured depth of somebody's cellar, offered as a rough guide.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are heard rather than spelt, and neither British spelling survives into the grid. Potential is the physicist's word for voltage, which is the quantity the instrument reads.
annotation.definitionFit: A voltmeter reads electrical potential across a circuit, so potential gauge describes the instrument by the quantity it measures.

entries.clue: Thief is central suspect (9)

indicatorNotes.suspect: Something suspect is not to be trusted as it stands, and letters not to be trusted are not standing in their right order.

blocks.note: two letters of fodder
seven letters of fodder, filling out the nine

annotation.surface: The person at the heart of the inquiry is the one the police like for it.
annotation.walkthrough: Suspect is the pivot: read as a noun it belongs to the police station, read as an adjective it is the instruction. Larceny is the legal name for theft, and the clue keeps that courtroom register in the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A larcenist is the person who commits larceny, the law's word for theft, so thief names the same person in plainer English.

entries.clue: Volcano found in Vietnam (4)

indicatorNotes.found in: Found in says the thing is already sitting inside the word beside it, waiting to be picked out rather than worked out.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters from the middle of the country's name: viETNAm

annotation.surface: A volcano discovered somewhere in Vietnam.
annotation.walkthrough: Vietnam does have volcanoes, which is what keeps the surface still; the one hiding in the letters is in Sicily. A hidden word this short usually needs a proper noun to sit in, since ordinary words rarely hold the right run.
annotation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano above Catania in Sicily, so volcano names it by its kind.

entries.clue: Invisible spirit, headless one creeps around (8)

indicatorNotes.headless: A headless word has lost the letter at its head, which is the first one it is written with.
indicatorNotes.around: Something moving around will not settle where it was put, so the letters are to be shifted out of the order given.

blocks.note: ONE with its first letter taken off, leaving two letters of fodder
six more letters of fodder, making eight in all

annotation.surface: A decapitated ghost creeping about the place, unseen.
annotation.walkthrough: Creeps looks like something the ghost is doing and is really the raw material, while around is the shuffle rather than the wandering. What people report feeling in an empty room is exactly the definition's invisible spirit.
annotation.definitionFit: A presence is the unseen something felt in a haunted room — there was a presence in there — which is the invisible spirit meant.

entries.clue: Point made another way (5-4)

indicatorNotes.made: To make a thing is to fashion it out of what you have, so the letters beside it are raw material to be set in a new order.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, resettled to open the answer
St is the abbreviation on street signs

annotation.surface: The same argument, put across in a different fashion.
annotation.walkthrough: Both everyday words swap to their map senses: point is a bearing rather than an argument, and way is a street rather than a manner. The hyphen in the enumeration is the join between the two halves.
annotation.definitionFit: North-east is the compass bearing midway between north and east, so point names it by its class.

entries.clue: Rule out a note in an introductory piece (8)

indicatorNotes.in: In sends the piece before it inside the words after it, splitting that longer word apart to make room.

blocks.note: a prelude is the short piece played before the main work
C is a note of the musical scale

annotation.surface: Striking out one note written into the opening movement.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is musical all the way through — note, introductory piece — and only the definition steps out of the concert hall. To preclude something is to shut it out in advance, not to cancel it afterwards.
annotation.definitionFit: To preclude an outcome is to make it impossible before it can arise, which is what ruling something out does.

entries.clue: Tradesperson to come in after fish (9)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the piece named last in the clue is the one written first.

blocks.note: the carp is a fat freshwater fish, and the crossword's default one
to come in is to enter

annotation.surface: A workman expected to arrive once the fish has been brought in.
annotation.walkthrough: Carp earns its keep twice over: short, vowel-light and also a verb meaning to grumble, so it can sit in a clue about complaining as easily as one about a river. The trade wanted works in wood.
annotation.definitionFit: A carpenter makes a living working wood — the chippie on a building site — so tradesperson names the job by its category.

entries.clue: Vehicle for two in violet and emerald (6)

indicatorNotes.in: In says the thing is inside the words that follow, written out in them already with nothing rearranged.

blocks.note: the run crosses two word joins: violeT AND EMerald

annotation.surface: A two-seater painted in violet and emerald.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition takes the first three words, which is why the hiding place starts so late in a clue this short. Picking a run that ends mid-word — emerald keeps four letters back — is what stops the join being obvious.
annotation.definitionFit: A tandem is the bicycle built for two, one saddle and one set of pedals behind the other, so vehicle for two names it exactly.

entries.clue: Roman soldiers with half their animals in bed? (6)

indicatorNotes.half: Half of a word is one of its two equal parts, and where the whole runs to six letters that part is three.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts what has gone before inside the word that follows, which splits to take it.

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
the soldiers' animals are horses, and the front half of that six-letter word is kept

annotation.surface: Legionaries turning in for the night with half their horses in the bed.
annotation.walkthrough: The animals are never named: Roman soldiers rode horses, and it is that unwritten word, not one in the clue, that gets halved. A cohort was a tenth of a legion, some five hundred men.
annotation.definitionFit: A cohort was one of the ten units a Roman legion was divided into, so Roman soldiers names the body of men the word describes.

entries.clue: Aran knit is stylish but rebellious (8)

indicatorNotes.knit: To knit is to work loose strands into new fabric, and letters worked over like that come out in an order of the setter's choosing.

blocks.note: the four letters of the islands' name reset; Aran is the group off the west coast of Ireland whose cable-knit jumpers are named after it
chic is stylish in the borrowed French sense

annotation.surface: A hand-knitted Aran jumper that looks smart but has a wild streak in it.
annotation.walkthrough: Aran knit reads as a kind of sweater and is really four letters and an instruction, which is the whole of the misdirection. Only the last word is left to define, and it sits where a solver expects an adjective about the jumper.
annotation.definitionFit: Anarchic means lawless and disorderly, refusing whatever authority is going, which is the rebellious sense wanted.

entries.clue: State of posh limo now and again (4)

indicatorNotes.now and again: Now and again means at intervals rather than all the time, so letters are taken from the words beside it every other one.

blocks.note: every second letter of the two words, starting with the second: pOsH lImO

annotation.surface: The condition of a rather grand car that is seen from time to time.
annotation.walkthrough: State looks like the condition the limo is in and is one of the fifty instead. Running the count straight through the space between the words is what lets two short words yield four letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Ohio is one of the United States, so the bare word state names it by its kind.

entries.clue: Upper hand in club once wicket's taken (4)

indicatorNotes.taken: Taken means carried off and gone, so the letter it names is lifted out of the word and never comes back.

blocks.note: a wedge is the golf club used to lift the ball steeply out of trouble
W is how a wicket is written on a cricket scoresheet, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: Gaining the advantage at the clubhouse the moment a batsman is out.
annotation.walkthrough: Two sports share the clue and neither belongs to the answer: the club is a golf iron and the wicket is the W on a cricket scorecard. To have the edge over a rival is to be narrowly ahead of them.
annotation.definitionFit: To have the edge on someone is to hold a slight advantage over them, the same standing the upper hand describes.

entries.clue: Made guests move inside when repelled (9)

indicatorNotes.move: Letters told to move do not stay where they were put, so they come back in a different order.
indicatorNotes.inside: Inside places the shuffled letters within the word already found, which splits apart to hold them.

blocks.note: made in the sense of did the deed, three letters that open and close the answer
the six letters reset before being dropped inside

annotation.surface: The guests were made to move indoors once something had driven them back.
annotation.walkthrough: Made is the past tense of do here, not of make, and that swap is the step most solvers reach last. Repelled works in two directions — pushed back, or turned off — and the definition wants the stomach rather than the battlefield.
annotation.definitionFit: To be disgusted is to be repelled by something in the sense of revolted by it, which is how the definition reads once the military sense is set aside.

entries.clue: Timid at the coconut stall (3)

annotation.definitionNote: The fairground stall is a coconut shy, so the clue hands over the first word of its name and asks for the second.

blocks.note: hanging back at a party, unwilling to meet anyone's eye
the fairground pitch with coconuts balanced on posts and wooden balls to throw at them

annotation.surface: Somebody hanging back nervously in front of the coconut stall at the fair.
annotation.walkthrough: A coconut shy is the stall itself, and a shy is also the throw you pay for — three balls for a pound. The timid sense is a separate word in the dictionary that happens to be spelt the same.
annotation.definitionFit: Shy means timid, as in a shy smile, and it is also the fairground throw and the stall named after it, the coconut shy.

entries.clue: Precious metal duck, gone! (3)

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, written on the card as a nought

annotation.surface: A little silver duck, and now it has vanished.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma invites you to read metal and duck as one ornament, and they are two separate pieces. A batsman out for no runs is said to be out for a duck, from duck's egg, the shape of the nought.
annotation.definitionFit: Ago marks time past — three weeks ago — and gone does the same work in six months gone, which is the sense the clue leans on.

entries.clue: Chaos when plant's in front of border (6)

indicatorNotes.in front of: In front of puts the piece it introduces first, with the one named next written behind it.

blocks.note: may is the hawthorn, the white hedgerow blossom named for the month it flowers in; the apostrophe-s is only is
a hem is the sewn border of a garment

annotation.surface: Trouble in the garden when the shrub ends up in front of the flowerbed.
annotation.walkthrough: The garden holds the surface together and neither half of the wordplay stays in it: the border is a sewn edge and the plant is the hawthorn. Mayhem originally meant maiming someone, and the violence has only partly worn off.
annotation.definitionFit: Mayhem is violent disorder, all hell breaking loose at once, which is what chaos names.

entries.clue: Get lost after command to trounce? (4,2)

blocks.note: what you say to somebody you want rid of — clear off, push off
an order to give something a thrashing, with the it taken literally as the thing to be beaten

annotation.surface: Being told to clear off once the order to thrash the opposition has gone out.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as a liberty: the it has no particular referent, it is just whatever is being beaten. Both readings are imperatives, which is what lets one sit behind the other in a single sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Beat it is an order to clear off, and read at face value it is an instruction to beat something — to trounce it.
